### 2026-10-27: # Oct 27: Parts, KiCad project and first schematic progress

**3h**

# Oct 27: Parts, KiCad project and first schematic progress

This week's theme is displays, so I wanted to further dwell into my nuclear energy interest (see my week 1 Geiger project!) and make something related. One of the coolest parts of any Nuclear Power Plant is obviously the Main Control Room, and it is full of annunciators. Walls of backlit tiles, and when something goes wrong, one of the tiles flashes and sounds an alarm until it is handled by the operator. So why not make it desk sized?

I've played a lot of nuclear related simulations, and I know roughly how they work. When a transient or other incident occurs, the relevant alarms start flashing fast. The operator can then press an ACK button to change the flashing to a steady state. After the condition is cleared (say your pressure was high and now it's okay), the tile flashes slowly until RESET is pressed. And there's our firmware! But that's work for later, we have the schematic to tackle first.

For the display side, I went with 12 backlit tiles, each with 5mm LEDs behind a 3d printed diffuser and a [seven segment display](https://www.gme.cz/v/1508913/led-displej-8x7-segmentu-cerveny) for CPM and uSv/h readings from my Geiger (yes, I'll try to connect them to add a high radiation alarm). The LEDs will be driven by two [shift registers](https://www.gme.cz/74hc595-dip16-texas-instruments) and it will all be controlled by a RPi Pico W, which I already have at home, so I can spare some money from the BOM!

![Picking out first parts](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/222b87a8dfb39ef9a040290e0500de1fe0deb0db3f8e300cd653e247a0ed7175.png)

When picking out the shift register, I originally wanted the 74HCT595 so that the chip could run at 5V and still be driven by 3.3V logic from the RPI, but sadly GM Electronic (my local electronics retailer) only had the HC variant and the HCT was available only as SMD, which I did not dare come close to after my Geiger project design (zero clue how I'm gonna solder that one..).

The HC version of the shift register needs logic inputs close to VCC, which means the entire chip has to run at 3.3V if we are using the RPi Pico. My red and yellow LEDs only need 2V forward voltage, so that's fine, but the white LEDs needed around 2.9V, which is too close and leaves almost no headroom.

I tried a few solutions (smaller resistor to let more current in?), but ended up connecting the anodes of the white LEDs to 5V instead of 3.3V. This means that when the shift register sets output to high, the voltage across the LED is only 1.7V and it shouldn't turn on. In the opposite scenario, when the output goes low, the LEDs should have no issue turning on.

In KiCad, I was able to tackle a good part of the schematic, mostly the pins of the Pico (ended up using 2x 1x20 socket connectors in place of the Pico as there wasn't a proper symbol for it I could find). I used the [Pico's datasheet](https://pip-assets.raspberrypi.com/categories/686-raspberry-pi-pico-w/documents/RP-008312-DS-2-pico-w-datasheet.pdf) to assign pins, and ended up assigning pins for the shift registers, the display and for the ACK/RESET/TEST buttons (test will light up all annunciators at once). I made a few mistakes and assigned to the wrong pins a few times, but checked my work and fixed it before it became an issue.

![Raspberry pi pico pins](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/4b4ed9c584a4be9c1bfb28e69625bd10774eebfdc6aec597d7f2e770fad84a00.png)

I also setup the two shift registers, chained them together, added a pull up resistor to make sure LEDs don't flash during boot and made the chain of 12 LEDs (the actual annunciator panels!). They were similar, but the resistor values and colors of the LEDs were different in each.

![Shift registers and LEDs](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/4581893c0d309612f2461a1802639e756da8b9bdf116d95e1131d4c4ebba42a2.png)

**tl;dr:** Sorted out parts for the project and established the concept and setup the pins for the Pico, handled shift registers (sorting out a voltage problem along the way) and made the LED chain.

**Time spent: ~3 hours**

**Next up:** Finishing the schematic.

### 2026-10-28: # Oct 28: Tackling issues from yesterday, finished schematic and started PCB

**6h**

# Oct 28: Tackling issues from yesterday, finished schematic and started PCB

I started today by fixing an issue I noticed from yesterday. In my schematic the white LEDs have their anodes on 5V, however, the shift register runs at 3.3 volts. I looked at the datasheet of the [74HC595](https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/sn74hc595.pdf) and it says that the voltage on any output pin must not go more than 0.5V above the VCC, yet we have a 1.7V difference on the 5V side.

To fix this, I added a transistor between each white LED and shift register. The output of the shift register now only drives the base of the transistor through a 10 kiloohm resistor, so the output pin never encounters the 5 volts we had before. I also added another 10k resistor pulling the base to ground to ensure it stays off during boot. However, we need to be careful when we make the firmware, as it means the white LED row now has inverted logic compared to red and yellow, and HIGH means on.

![Revised white LEDs](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/513a5780f083e3e23f726cd26a46234104565c3193dfb07b418a9371eb4c14bd.png)

After this fix, I finished the rest of the schematic, mainly the MAX7219 display module which connects through a 5 pin socket. Originally I planned to have a second socket to support the other end of the module, but encountered an issue where I don't know the exact size of the module. Some manufacturers list it as 80mm, some list 85mm, so I would have to guess. Instead, I completely removed the second socket and decided I will sit the other end on a 3D printed support bracket.

The speaker circuit has a 2N3904 transistor switching my KSSG3108 speaker via a 47 ohm resistor. This way we stay within its 0.1W rating. I also had to make a custom footprint from the datasheet for it, as it isn't a standard part in KiCad.

![Speaker, display and button section](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/cfde54611c21619b04ac62b2744d01ae6e239ae7c1897897790d63dfcdde4df0.png)

![Finished schematic](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/b71cf7bec0d9f113fbb8369ff2c33f7d19bcd51f0ca1ea5f545d1f2e8d011697.png)

I added the three buttons (ACK, RESET and TEST) which was quite simple and then moved onto assigning footprints for the PCB. This was a bit trickier. As with every other project I've done so far, the auto suggestions from KiCad were wrong. I had to fix each one manually.

![Incorrect footprint suggestions from KiCad](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/b4ad9d604a2f19a0e7745c66de5eb4ae82ca9fb2248bcda4ddb0f5981cb83ff8.png)

![Finished footprint assignments](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/38fc0a63649012cf6f0ba77367a421c9467ec233169e5441db610405299bd8a8.png)

![Custom speaker footprint](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/905318fa9a6e513c89617708ca6a71df93537071e92b635b995a87d9720bcc4c.png)

Then I started the PCB layout. I quickly realized everything wouldn't fit on one side of a 100x100mm board, so I decided I would place the 12 LEDs on the front and keep most electronics on the back side. This was a bit new to me, as all previous projects used previously only used one side of the PCB for components. The placement of the back side isn't the prettiest, but it should work.

I also setup design rules to define clearance and track size, and began some routing. I routed each LED to its resistor and did most of the routing from the TILE lines on each LED to the shift registers, which was a bit tricky on the white LEDs as they also have the transistor. So far, the design rules checker didn't notice any issues.

![Configured design rules](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/dcab575d4a97ba8fa3b93d3d58d70c3682b904645c3308935d29c8214cebc15c.png)

![Component placement and routing progress](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/11a83e3ef468ac93410c75928c5a4f5cafb51c4022b28f535118def7a9b767df.png)

![Front side 3D Render so far](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/ff2d89f31dfe33690e05098267035e54efaec23bc6b24d2dbb8e3a60402aa241.png)

![Back side 3D Render so far](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/77820b3558f21155a025e06d4e8cf6262972f74c0791b229ba8fc9ec1e772f45.png)

**tl;dr: Fixed an issue with the white LED voltage, finished the schematic, made a custom footprint for the speaker, assigned footprints, placed all parts on the PCB and began routing.**

**Total time spent: ~6 hours**

**Next up: Finishing routing, ground pour**

### 2026-10-29: # Oct 29: Fixing issues, finishing routing, exporting gerbers and CAD work

**6h**

# Oct 29: Fixing issues, finishing routing, exporting gerbers and CAD work

The first thing I did today was fix another issue from yesterday. I looked at the datasheet of the seven segment display I'm using ([MAX7219](https://www.analog.com/media/en/technical-documentation/data-sheets/MAX7219-MAX7221.pdf)) and it turns out that it needs 3.5 volts for a HIGH input, yet our RPI Pico only outputs 3.3 volts. I decided I would build a small level shifter from some extra parts I had in my GM cart (I had some extra transistors and resistors due to minimum order quantities). I used three 2N3904 transistors each with a 1k resistor on the base and another pullup to 5 volts on the collector.

Again a similar issue as with the white LEDs occurs here that each transistor will invert the signal, meaning the display will see a LOW when the Pico sends a HIGH. Thankfully it should just be a few lines of code in the firmware so no big deal.

![Level shifter in my schematic](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/1390e22c64c9d800f58bb9eb1a96c0a5c86a406665dfc723cefd3d4d3ae509a2.png)

After that I added the shifter components to the PCB and continued routing. This took arguably the longest as there was A LOT of components that were really cramped, but I managed to route it and get rid of all the ratslines. After finishing the routing, I did the ground pour to connect all the GND pads and ran DRC. For the first time while working on Half Life, I got a clean DRC after a ground pour! This made me very happy, usually I had some unconnected islands or spots the pour couldn't reach but it was perfect today.

![Routed board](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/16f3c99d068d947da5438c2888bc717a039b70cdeee943963184b9f340398ae0.png)

![Ground pour](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/48482d5dab56beb1b82a1059ac7c84895580643554d8b5d5d614ca77f986a6d3.png)

![Clean DRC](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/56debee9e05a2d93570a58754bf6ff869c0f44c918aaf133c04c1f835e6c0767.png)

Afterwards, I exported Gerbers and checked JLCPCB for a quote. Just like my other projects, the 100x100 board 5x came out to around 15$ with shipping, which was roughly what I expected. There are also some coupons available but I'm not sure if they will still be available when I'm ordering the board or whether they won't be used up on  my other orders.

![PCB quote](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/d045a78b92a5222b32d07337be5ee62380fe632ab7f334a7d011f4ac1986981d.png)

With all KiCad work done, I also exported a STEP file and imported it to Autodesk Fusion to work on the enclosure. I made a 105 milimeter by 105 milimeter box. Then I cut 12 windows for each annunciator pane and a window for the seven segment displays. I also made a second grid with each cell slightly larger than the inner window and extruded it down to stop 3 milimeters above the PCB. I originally tried 2 milimeters, but Fusion's interference checker found issues, so I shortened it a bit.

![Imported PCB in Fusion](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/89e45ff3104dbac26b2bcbc79fe4548e49cadbf386429ffed8f4a38bcaaf1722.png)

![Interference](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/00c2bf62867ad6aab7d9201655843ef7896d0ea2a93281e8c7a18a5ebb264e22.png)

![Today's CAD progress](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/9555c3c19e4cfb09c0623ce0acd879bf506645727604242f048f53528bc15438.png)

**tl;dr: Built level shifters using transistors for the seven segment display, finished all routing, did the ground pour, exported Gerbers, got a JLCPCB quote, started Fusion enclosure work with the shell, tile and display windows and extruded grid.**

**Time spent: ~6 hours**

**Next up: Finishing the enclosure and CAD work**

### 2026-10-30: # Oct 30: CAD work and firmware

**6h**

# Oct 30: CAD work and firmware

Most of today's work happened in Autodesk Fusion where I finished designing the enclosure for 3D printing. Yesterday I only made the basic shell with windows for the tiles and display but today I finished it so it can actually be assembled.

First I worked on the buttons, I added a plunger above each button on the PCB that reaches through the front plate, it is a 6 milimeter rod with a slightly bigger flange making sure it doesn't fall out. I made the rod 0.4 milimeters smaller than the hole and had to be a bit careful about dimensions to make sure it doesn't bind nor wobble.

![Button plunger design](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/50043d1acc04a1e9e75ac0adb3b725ba0e21927028e57404ffacdd9cadfb32b6.png)

I then made the speaker grill, which was just a circular pattern of holes in the front plate. I made one center hole and two rings, one with 6 holes and the other with 12 holes which came out to 19 holes total. Next, I had to tackle handling the 7 segment display module. It plugs in only on one end into J3, so I need to hold it up with something on the other end. I made a small extruded circle with a pin on top of it which will go into the seven segment display module's mounting hole (in the corner). It's a separate part so if the hole ends up in a different spot I can adjust and reprint it. I was originally going to design the PCB so it would hold the display, but each store I looked at listed slightly different specs or dimensions for the display and if I went with the wrong one, it wouldn't work properly after my PCB was assembled. This way, in the worst case scenario, I can easily adjust.

![Speaker grill](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/6981e9343ef9cd2ce4956afab84c32cb9fe68b03d9e5bb2c131550f4eb28b6a1.png)

![Display holding pin](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/96775b553a23df67629d4f137920a6a254a8a08fc6da6c08513a22519856b76e.png)

Then I made the diffuser tiles. I made 12 tiles each sitting in one of the windows. They will be printed in white PLA to let the LED light through, and the label paper will be placed on them.

![Diffusers](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/905326f36c9ed4241665a0e3ed286f18dce4f8947c7130feeed492df3d3b5e4f.png)

The hardest part was deciding how I would hold the PCB inside the enclosure. In the end, I made 4 small ledges on the inside of the bezel walls that I will rest the PCB against, and made a back cover with 4 posts in the corners (extruded circles) that press against the board. The back cover has two small flexible arms with small hooks that click into slots that I cut through the enclosure. I wanted to avoid screws to reduce my BOM a little. I ran Fusion's interference and it only found some interference on the PCB but that's likely from the KiCad export itself from the components and doesn't really matter to me. Lastly, I made the cutout for the USB port of the RPI Pico.

![Ledges and posts](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/472f4b5dbd64c95a17b91088b6f1a85a7ba428cd3d0f64d99b8733de72f1abf9.png)

![USB port cutout](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/3e924f759af688fae488c87db963dfec5210baf7ca5e28de27dcbb41e1478ec8.png)

![Final enclosure model](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/65de21ea76af34df536da241d2c9c45543063ee663f9ed824a13aebcff97ee08.png)

I continued today's work by making the printable label sheets for each of the tiles and started work on the firmware. I made a small test in CircuitPython. The shift registers use SPI to send 16 bits (the first 8 tiles on U1 and the remaining 4 ones on U2). It took me a while to figure out the white tiles because due to my changes from 1 or 2 days ago, their logic is inverted so we need to flip it in the code as well. For the yellow and red rows, setting the bit to 0 turns it on and 1 turns it off, whereas for the white ones it works the exact opposite. I made it so we check if the tile index is 8 or more and flip the logic if so. My test lights each tile one by one and has a loop which lets the user toggle the lights with the buttons, which isn't the intended functionality yet, but I wanted to mostly get an idea of how the lighting will work in CircuitPython so I made a small demo. I will build on top of it tomorrow. While working on this journal entry, I actually noticed that my firmware already had a bug, and the inverter logic was opposite! I inverted the inverter logic, that's quite the problem. Anyway, I fixed it and committed it, I just had to swap the two branches.

![Basic firmware test](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/9378e917da0d9196f0d70ddb1bfb49d52cae58550e6084cfb38c0a9c9b66036e.png)

**tl;dr: Finished all CAD work (entire enclosure with button plungers, speaker grill, display supports, diffuser tiles, back cover and USB cutout), created labels and made the initial test for the firmware.**

**Time spent: ~6 hours**

**Next up: Finishing the firmware and project completion**
